semantic_correction.stem: A telephone-triage RN receives a caller reporting new chest pressure with shortness of breath that began about 10 minutes ago. Which action is most appropriate?

options.A: Tell the caller the symptoms are probably cardiac and recommend being driven to the nearest emergency department for evaluation.
options.B: Use focused triage questions to recognize the possible emergency and direct immediate EMS activation according to the authorized protocol.
options.C: Obtain a complete medical and family history before deciding whether the caller needs emergency transport or a same-day clinic visit.
options.D: Advise the caller to take aspirin and rest for 15 minutes, then activate EMS if the chest pressure and shortness of breath do not improve.

semantic_correction.rationale: NHLBI identifies chest pain, heaviness, or discomfort and shortness of breath as heart-attack warning symptoms and advises calling 9-1-1 for emergency medical care even when the person is not certain that a heart attack is occurring. NHLBI also states that an ambulance is the safest way to reach the hospital and that calling 9-1-1 should not be delayed to take aspirin or try another measure first. The 2026 NCSBN NCLEX-RN Test Plan expects the RN to prioritize care based on acuity, assess referral needs, use resources, and practice within legal scope. Option B uses focused triage only to identify the time-sensitive risk and directs EMS activation under the authorized protocol without making a definitive remote diagnosis. A labels the symptoms as probably cardiac and substitutes private transport for EMS. C delays emergency action for a comprehensive history that is not needed before referral. D delays EMS while trying aspirin and rest first. Therefore B is the uniquely best answer.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: In telephone triage, recognize new chest pressure with shortness of breath as a possible time-sensitive emergency and direct immediate EMS activation according to authorized protocol without making a definitive remote diagnosis or delaying for treatment trials.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: retained the valid telephone-triage emergency construct, removed the uniquely-longest correct-answer cue, normalized difficulty from hard to medium, and rebuilt the responses so the RN recognizes a possible emergency and activates EMS under authorized protocol without diagnosing ACS or delaying emergency referral for history-taking or aspirin.

audit_findings_append.finding: The original answer was conspicuously longest. The revised item preserves the NHLBI-supported emergency referral while explicitly keeping the RN within triage recognition/protocol scope rather than remote diagnosis or unauthorized treatment.
audit_findings_append.blueprint_locator: Management of Care — acuity prioritization, referrals/resources, legal scope

option_audit.A: Plausible because urgent emergency-department evaluation is appropriate, but the nurse should not make even a probable cardiac diagnosis from the call, and NHLBI identifies EMS/ambulance as the safest transport for suspected heart attack.
option_audit.B: Correct. It performs only enough triage to recognize the possible emergency and immediately routes the caller to EMS under an authorized protocol.
option_audit.C: Plausible because history is part of triage, but a complete lifetime/family history would delay emergency referral despite current warning symptoms.
option_audit.D: Plausible because aspirin can be used in some cardiac emergencies, but NHLBI explicitly advises not delaying the 9-1-1 call to take aspirin or try another measure first.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. The caller has new chest pressure plus shortness of breath. B is the only option that recognizes the possible emergency without making a definitive diagnosis and initiates immediate EMS referral. A uses private transport and diagnostic labeling; C and D delay EMS.

cueing_check.note: Exact character counts were calculated from the stored strings. B and D are exactly equal in length and all four options are complete triage responses; the correct answer is not uniquely longest.
